findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the gate-YAML `uses:` scanner must recursively walk ALL nested step frames (branch `then:`/`else:` arms, etc.) — not just the top-level `steps:` list — and cite the traversal strategy (e.g. a recursive helper or `re.findall(r'uses:\s+(\S+)', yaml_text)` on the raw text) so the implementation cannot silently cover only 1 of the 9 `uses:` references.
evidence: plan-review.yaml: `plan_review_precheck` at top-level step; ALL others (plan_review_assemble_criteria, plan_review_grounding, plan_review_verify_inputs, plan_review_decide, plan_review_coach_inputs, plan_review_coach x3, plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs) nested inside branch.then / branch.else frames

The plan's own cited proof — 'plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs already lives in another module while referenced at plan-review.yaml:136' — is itself a nested step (inside branch.then), so the guard must recurse to reach even the plan's own example
Plan says 'location-independent by construction' but does not specify the traversal strategy (recursive dict walk, YAML grep, etc.)
findings.finding: The gate-YAML `uses:` resolution check (AC3 / Testing section) has a mechanism-correctness gap: nearly all `uses:` steps in `plan-review.yaml` are nested 3-4 levels deep inside `branch.then` / `branch.else` arms, not at the top-level `steps:` list. A naive implementation that iterates `workflow['steps']` without recursive descent would silently miss 7 of the 9 `uses:` references (plan_review_grounding, plan_review_verify_inputs, plan_review_decide, plan_review_coach_inputs, plan_review_coach x3 coach arms), producing a guard that stays green even when those ops vanish from the registry — the exact defect it exists to catch.
findings.location: Testing section, paragraph 3 ('assert every `uses:` in `gates/plan-review.yaml` is present in `STEP_REGISTRY`'); also AC item 3
scenarios: An implementer writes `for step in yaml.safe_load(yaml_text)['steps']` with no recursion, covers only `plan_review_precheck`, and the test passes vacuously — the guard cannot detect removal of plan_review_decide or plan_review_coach from the registry
A future branch restructure of plan-review.yaml adds another nesting level; a non-recursive parser silently stops covering newly-nested steps
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Testing section: 'The `uses:` extractor must recurse into `branch.then`, `branch.else`, `loop.steps`, and any other nested frame keys — a flat `steps:` scan covers only `plan_review_precheck`. The simplest correct implementation is `re.findall(r"^\s+uses:\s+(\S+)", yaml_text, re.MULTILINE)` on the raw YAML text, which is structure-independent and therefore truly location-independent.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a falsifiability requirement to AC item 3: either (a) require a concrete assertion that the parsed `uses:` set from `gates/plan-review.yaml` has the expected cardinality (e.g., assert `len(uses_steps) >= N` for a known N, so an empty-parse is immediately red), or (b) require recording that the check goes red when a synthetic unknown step name is injected into the parsed YAML set — analogous to the deletion experiment in AC item 2.
evidence: AC item 2: 'PROVE IT BITES, and prove it in the subprocess form: with the `:45` import removed, the check must report `plan_review_prerequisite_verify_inputs` missing'
AC item 3: 'a test asserts every `uses:` in `gates/plan-review.yaml` is present in `STEP_REGISTRY`, RUN IN THE SAME SUBPROCESS ISOLATION' — no analogous falsifiability experiment required

Absence of any AC requiring: (a) verification that the YAML parser extracts the correct count/set of `uses:` values, or (b) a probe showing the check goes red when a synthetic unknown step is added to the YAML or a registered step is removed
findings.finding: The gate-YAML resolution test (AC item 3) has no falsifiability / failure-mode requirement analogous to AC item 2. AC item 2 explicitly requires proving the registry-membership check goes red when the `workflow_ops.py:45` import is deleted and recording both observations. AC item 3 imposes no equivalent obligation — it only mandates subprocess isolation. A gate-YAML check could be written with subtly wrong YAML parsing (e.g., failing to extract all `uses:` fields), an empty parsed step list, or a comparison that is always vacuously true, and the AC would be satisfied while the check detects nothing.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — AC item 3 (gate-YAML resolution check)
scenarios: Developer writes the gate-YAML check but mis-parses the YAML (e.g., misses nested `uses:` fields or iterates the wrong key), producing an empty set that is trivially a subset of STEP_REGISTRY — check always passes regardless of actual YAML content

Developer writes the check correctly but a future YAML restructure moves `uses:` to a new nesting level — the check silently stops exercising any steps and no one notices because no falsifiability probe exists
findings.suggested_fix: Extend AC item 3 with a sentence such as: 'Additionally, assert that the set of `uses:` values extracted from the YAML is non-empty and matches the expected count; record that the check goes red when a step name not present in STEP_REGISTRY is substituted into the parsed set — this is the analogue of the AC item 2 deletion experiment and proves the YAML-parsing path is live.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a note to AGENTS.md (or equivalent persistent design doc) recording that step-registry membership checks MUST use subprocess isolation — not in-process — because STEP_REGISTRY is a process-global populated at import time and will appear pre-populated in any normal pytest run.
evidence: AC 2(a): 'the new test module's docstring states that an in-process assertion stays green when the workflow_ops.py:45 import is deleted, and therefore why the subprocess form is mandatory'
No mention of AGENTS.md / ADR / design-doc update anywhere in the plan

The plan itself says 'STEP_REGISTRY is a process-global dict (executor.py:155) populated as an IMPORT SIDE EFFECT' — this is a non-obvious architectural constraint that will trap the next person who adds a registry guard in-process
findings.finding: The subprocess isolation pattern for registry membership checks is a novel testing contract that future contributors must replicate for any new step-registry guard, but the plan does not require updating AGENTS.md or an equivalent persistent design document — only the test module docstring and a ticket comment.
scenarios: A future engineer adds a new step-registry membership check in-process (the 'obvious' way), it passes CI, and silently fails to catch a missing registration — replicating the exact defect this ticket exists to prevent.
The test docstring is the only persistent record; if the test is deleted or rewritten without the docstring, the constraint is lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a single bullet to AGENTS.md under a 'Testing patterns' or 'Seam tests' section: 'Step-registry membership assertions must run in a subprocess (`subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", ...])`); an in-process check reads an already-populated STEP_REGISTRY and cannot detect a missing registration import. See `tests/unit/test_plan_review_workflow_ops_seam.py` for the canonical pattern.'

findings.finding: AC #2 requires that the in-process membership check 'stay green under that deletion' be 'recorded as evidence', but the plan never specifies the concrete artifact or mechanism: is this a code comment, a dedicated test function marked xfail/skip, or a prose note in the PR? Without a stated form, an executing agent cannot know whether CI enforces it or not, and 'shown to stay green' is not a proving command.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria – AC #2; Testing section ('record both observations rather than only the red one')
findings.suggested_fix: Add to AC #2: 'Record the in-process observation as a commented-out code block plus docstring note directly below the subprocess assertion, explicitly stating the output seen when run without the side-effect import. CI need not enforce this half; the subprocess test is the enforced guard.' This makes the documentary intent explicit and removes ambiguity about whether a second test function is required.

findings.finding: AC3's gate-YAML resolution test is not specified to run in a subprocess with a clean sys.modules, yet it depends on the same process-global STEP_REGISTRY that AC1 mandates subprocess isolation for. The plan's own argument — 'STEP_REGISTRY is a process-global dict populated as an IMPORT SIDE EFFECT, and at least six test modules already import rebar.llm.workflow.steps … deleting the registration import at workflow_ops.py:45 would NOT turn it red' — applies with equal force to an in-process gate-YAML check: if the side-effect import is removed, the registry is already populated by earlier test-session imports and the AC3 assertion stays green, making it a decorative guard that cannot detect the defect it exists for.
